passage: Tomas had a plan, written in green pen on a card: invite both parents to the same football match and sit them together. The stadium in Valencia was loud and sunny. His mum arrived first, then his dad, and they sat with one empty seat between them, polite as strangers. Tomas watched them instead of the game. On the tram home, his older brother Mateo said, "You can't fix it, you know. It's not your job." Tomas stared out the window. "I know," he said at last, "but I hoped." Mateo put an arm around him. The next Saturday Tomas went to a match with his dad and just enjoyed the goals.

qa.q: What did Tomas write his plan on?
qa.a: He wrote it in green pen on a card.

qa.q: What did Tomas hope would happen when he invited both parents to the match?
qa.a: He was hoping they would sit together and get back together, which is why he watched them instead of the game.

qa.q: What might help Tomas as he slowly accepts things?
qa.a: He can enjoy time with each parent separately, as he did with his dad at the next match, and talk with Mateo about his hope.

qa.q: How might Mateo see Tomas's plan?
qa.a: Mateo sees that fixing it is not Tomas's job and says so gently, then comforts him with an arm around him, so he seems kind rather than harsh.

grounding: A child hopes to reunite his parents through a plan, learns he cannot fix it, and accepts it slowly.

passage:
"Aparna, your Joseph Uncle had a plan once. My parents had separated when I was ten, and I was sure I could fix it. I decided on a family photo day. I rang the studio and booked it myself, told each of them the other had agreed.
They both came. They were polite. They stood stiffly for the photo. Then they went home to separate houses.
I cried that night. But later I saw something. My father taught me chess on Saturdays. My mother and I baked on Sundays. Each day was good, just different.
Once I stopped trying to fix them, I could enjoy each of them."

qa.q: What did young Joseph book at the studio?
How did young Joseph feel after the photo day?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad, crying that night because his plan didn't bring his parents back together.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Joseph?
qa.a: Seeing that he couldn't fix his parents' marriage and starting to enjoy chess with his father and baking with his mother.

qa.q: How might Joseph's parents have felt standing for the photo?
qa.a: They likely felt awkward and stiff, trying to be polite for their son's sake.

grounding: An uncle recalls hoping to reunite his separated parents with a plan, being disappointed, and slowly accepting so he could enjoy time with each.

passage:
Parul had planned everything for her birthday: both parents at the same table, a cake with both their names on the card. Maybe, if they sat together, they'd remember.
But it rained, the roads flooded, and Papa was an hour late. By the time he arrived, Charu, her mother, had already cut the cake with the cousins.
Papa sat at the far end. They were polite, but didn't talk.
Parul went to the balcony. Her throat ached.
Papa came out. "Birthday walk tomorrow? Just us?" Then Charu came out with a plate. "Your favourite piece, with the rose."
Parul realised: two separate, happy moments. Not the one she'd planned. But still happy.

qa.q: Why was Papa an hour late?
qa.a: It rained and the roads flooded.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling on the balcony?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and sad, with an aching throat, because her plan to bring her parents together hadn't worked.

qa.q: What did Parul start to accept?
qa.a: That she couldn't fix her parents' marriage, but she could enjoy separate happy moments with each of them.

qa.q: How might Charu feel bringing Parul the rose piece of cake?
qa.a: Charu probably wants Parul to feel loved on her birthday, even if things can't be the way Parul hoped.

grounding: A girl hopes her separated parents will reunite at her birthday; when her plan fails, she begins to accept it and enjoy time with each.
